Mr. Geraint Howells asked the Secretary of State for Wales if then: are any plans to build a dual carriageway in Mid-Wales during the next five years; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Michael Roberts: Work has recently been completed on the Brecon southern bypass which is a dual carriageway. Short lengths of dual carriageway astride junctions are also incorporated in the Dolgellau bypass which is due to be opened next spring and some dual 324 carriageway trunk road is being considered for the Welshpool relief roads scheme. The actual date of starts for the latter scheme is dependent on the satisfactory completion of the statutory procedures and on the availability of funds at that time. Generally speaking, however, traffic needs on trunk roads in Mid-Wales are met by the provision of good standard single carriageway roads.
Mr. Geraint Howells asked the Secretary of State for Wales if he is satisfied with local authorities' housing policy in Wales; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Wyn Roberts: I am studying the policies of the Welsh local authorities as expressed in their latest housing strategy and investment programme submissions. My first impression is that, in general, they are formulating their policies in a responsible way.
Sir Raymond Gower asked the Secretary of State for Wales what external financing limit and what target rate of return will be applied to the Welsh Water Authority in 1981–82.

Mr. Nicholas Edwards: The external financing limit for the Welsh Water Authority will be £29 million in 1981–82. Water authorities are being set financial targets in the form of a rate of current cost operating profit on the current value of their net assets. The WWA will be required to earn 0·3 per cent. in 1981–82 as the first step towards achieving a target of 1·25 per cent. by 1985–86.
I know that the WWA is examining its budget for next year with the utmost care, to ensure that increases in charges are kept to the lowest level.

Mr. Freud asked the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food (1) if he will amend his current legislation to enable the Meat and Livestock Commission to levy producers for the specific purpose of eradicating Aujeszky's disease;
(2) if he will conduct a poll among pig producers to ascertain the level of support for a self-funded scheme to eradicate Aujeszky's disease.
Mr. Peter Walker: I refer the hon. Member to the replies that I gave to him and to my hon. Friend the Member for Eye (Mr. Gummer) on 4 December.

14. Miss Joan Lestor asked the Secretary of State for Employment what studies have been made by his Department of the increased number of school leavers to enter the labour market in the first half of the 1980s as a result of the increase in the number of births in the 1960s.

Mr. Jim Lester: The Government have estimates of the numbers of school leavers entering the labour market
325 in successive academic years. The number is expected to peak at 715,000 in the current academic year and to decline thereafter. My Department has sponsored a number of research projects into the experience of school leavers entering the labour market.
17. Mrs. Dunwoody asked the Secretary of State for Employment how many special schemes for school leavers will be implemented in the Crewe travel-to-work area in the year 1980–81.

Mr. Jim Lester: I am informed by the Manpower Services Commission that in the Crewe and Nantwich local authority district, which roughly approximates to the Crewe travel-to-work area, there were 600 places on approved schemes at the end of October 1980. Some 420 young people had already entered YOP by that date. The commission will keep the stock of places under review to ensure that no young person in the groups covered by the undertaking will be left without the offer of a place on the programme.

15. Sir David Price asked the Secretary of State for Employment what steps he is taking to ensure a closer liaison between the training boards and his Department on the one hand and schools on the other on the employment qualifications for young people.

Mr. Mayhew: The Manpower Services Commission (MSC), the industrial training boards and the Education Departments already work closely together on this important question, and my right hon. Friend is encouraging this. The Department of Employment and the Department of Education and Science now work more closely in this field than ever before.
16. Mr. Foulkes asked the Secretary of State for Employment what is the current estimated number of employees on short-time working in the United Kingdom; and how this compares with November 1979.

Mr. Jim Lester: Information is available only for operatives in manufacturing industries in Great Britain. The numbers on short-time working, either for the whole or for part of the week in the weeks ended 13 September 1980 and 10 November 1979, were 368,000 and 64,700, respectively.

18. Mr. Chapman asked the Secretary of State for Employment if he is satisfied with the work being undertaken by jobcentres with particular reference to their cost effectiveness and placing of people in new jobs as compared with the old employment exchanges.

Mr. Jim Lester: I am generally satisfied with the work being undertaken by jobcentres. Jobcentres are more cost effective than the old employment exchanges, they are helping to place people in employment more quickly and the atmosphere they engender for job seekers has greatly improved. The increased volume of business handled by jobcentres means that staff productivity is higher and cost per placing lower than in other offices. Evaluation has also shown that, compared with the offices they replace, 326 jobcentres handle more vacancies, fill more of the vacancies notified to them and place more job seekers into employment.
Mr. Latham asked the Secretary of State for Employment whether he will make a statement on the future role of jobcentres.
30. Mr. Kenneth Lewis asked the Secretary of State for Employment what instructions he has given to the Manpower Services Commission in respect of the opening of new jobcentres.

Mr. Jim Lester: I have informed the Manpower Services Commission that I support its jobcentre programme and its plans to complete it. However, the future pace of this programme will be affected by the resources available to the commission.

43. Mr. McQuarrie asked the Secretary of State for Employment what proposals he has for closing the jobcentres and reverting to the practice that all job vacancies are dealt with by local employment offices.

Mr. Jim Lester: Until 1972 vacancies notified to the public employment service were handled in offices which also dealt with the payment of unemployment benefit. I have no proposals for reverting to that system, or for a general policy of closing jobcentres. Since modernisation, the public employment service has performed more efficiently. In particular, jobcentres, which are replacing the old style employment offices, handle more vacancies, fill more of the vacancies notified to them, place more jobseekers into employment and do so at a lower unit cost than the offices they are replacing. As a result, I have informed the Manpower Services Commission that I support its jobcentre programme and its plans to complete it. However, the future pace of the MSC's jobcentre programme will be determined in the light of resources available to the commission. I have also asked the MSC to develop the programme of modernising the employment service in the most cost-effective way and to avoid extravagance particularly in relation to the siting of jobcentres.
19. Mr. Barry Jones asked the Secretary of State for Employment what is his estimate of the rise in unemployment in the United Kingdom since May 1979.
Mr. Prior: Between May 1979 and November 1980 the increase in the numbers registered as unemployed in the United Kingdom, seasonally adjusted and excluding school leavers, was 722,100.
37. Mr. Ashley asked the Secretary of State for Employment if he will make a statement on the current level of unemployment.
Mr. Jim Lester: At 13 November 1980 the number of people registered as unemployed in the United Kingdom was 2,162,874 compared with 1,355,203 at 8 November 1979.
Mr. Archie Hamilton asked the Secretary of State for Employment how many people were in employment in each year since 1945, subdivided between men and women, part-timers and full-timers.

Mr. Jim Lester: Comprehensive estimates of the numbers of all male and female employees in employment
327 are available from mid-1948 to 1980 and of full-time and part-time employees from mid-1971 to 1977. The following table gives the available information for Great Britain.
1. Estimates from 1948 to 1959(a) are based on mid-year counts of national insurance cards.

2. Figures from 1971 to 1977 are from censuses of employment. Those from 1959(b) to 1970, taken from the continuous series of employment estimates, are comparable with the census figures and take account of discontinuities present in earlier data.
3. Figures for 1978, 1979 and 1980 are from the quarterly series of provisional employment estimates which does not distinguish full-time from part-time employees.
20. Mr. Dubs asked the Secretary of State for Employment how many people are currently on youth opportunities programme schemes in inner London; and how many eligible for such schemes are unemployed.

Mr. Jim Lester: I am informed by the Manpower Services Commission that there were some 2,200 young people participating in the youth opportunities programme and 9,320 registered with more than six weeks unemployment at the October count in Inner London Education Authority boroughs

Mr. Alton asked the Secretary of State for Employment what is the current amount payable in training allowance to a 19-year-old trainee on the youth opportunities programme; and if he will make a statement on how this relates to unemployment pay and supplementary benefits and its effect on whether or not trainees are attracted to the scheme.

Mr. Jim Lester: I am informed by the MSC that the allowance payable to trainees in the youth opportunities programme is £23·50 a week. This compares with the following benefits paid to 19 year olds:
Unemployment benefit (single person) £20·65
Supplementary benefit (single, non householder) £19·20

The youth opportunities programme has been for 16 to 18-year-olds, although in certain circumstances some 19-year-olds whose entry to the employment market has been delayed for reasons other than continuing formal education could be admitted to the programme. Following my right hon. Friend's announcement on 21 November 1980—[Vol. 994, c. 204–7]—the youth opportunities programme will be focused on 16 and 17-year-olds, although young people up to the age of 24 will be eligible for entry if places are available and it is considered it would be of significant benefit to their employment prospects.

21. Mr. Gwilym Roberts asked the Secretary of State for Employment what are the latest figures available for the number of people unemployed and working short time; what were the equivalent figures a year ago; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Jim Lester: At 13 November 1980 the number of people registered as unemployed in the United Kingdom was 2,162,874 compared with 1,355.203 at 8 November 1979.

Information on short time working is available only for operatives in manufacturing industries in Great Britain. The numbers on short time either for the whole or part of the week, in the weeks ended 13 September 1980 and 8 September 1979 were 368,000 and 51,100, respectively.

The high level of unemployment imposes great individual hardship and great economic cost. We are tackling this by bringing down inflation and reducing public spending so that industry has the confidence and resources to invest in the future. In the meantime we have expanded the special employment measures to help those most affected by unemployment.
22. Mr. Hooley asked the Secretary of State for Employment what amount of the extol money allocated to the Manpower Services Commission for 1980–81 will be devoted to industrial training.
Mr. Jim Lester: No extra money is being allocated to the Manpower Services Commission for industrial training in 1980–81.

23. Mr. Haselhurst asked the Secretary of State for Employment if he is satisfied with monitoring procedures for participants in training and work experience schemes funded by the Manpower Services Commission.

Mr. Jim Lester: I am informed by the Manpower Services Commission that detailed monitoring procedures have been drawn up to ensure that training and work experience schemes funded under the youth opportunities
329 programmes are operating correctly. Resources constraints have led to some reduction in the frequency of monitoring visits, but the matter is kept under constant review.

24. Mr. Jim Marshall asked the Secretary of State for Employment what estimate he has made the employment effect of the economic package announced by the Chancellor of the Exchequer on Monday 24 November.
Mr. Jim Lester: I refer the hon. Member to the reply given earlier by my right hon. Friend to the hon. Member for Harlow (Mr. Newens).
25. Mr. van Straubenzee asked the Secretary of State for Employment when next he plans to meet the leaders of the Trades Union Congress to discuss the present employment situation.

Mr. Jim Lester: The employment situation was discussed by all parties on the National Economic Development Council on 3 December. My right hon. Friend expects further such discussions with leaders of the Trades Union Congress in the coming months.

26. Mr. Dalyell asked the Secretary of State for Emloyment how much money is being allocated to the work of environmental improvement programmes, pursuant to his statement, Official Report, column 224, 21 November.

Mr. Jim Lester: I am informed by the Manpower Services Commission that no fixed allocation of community enterprise programme funds is to be made between schemes for the improvement of the environment and other schemes of benefit to the community. Every scheme proposed by a sponsor will be equally considered on its merits.

27. Mr. Knox asked the Secretary of State for Employment when he proposes to have further consultations with the Confederation of British Industry about the long-term improvement of industrial relations.

Mr. Mayhew: My right hon. Friend has had a number of discussions with representatives of the Confederation of British Industry about the long-term improvement of industrial relations. He is, of course, ready to meet them at any time.

28. Mr. Hardy asked the Secretary of State for Employment how many young persons are currently unemployed in the county of South Yorkshire; and how this compares with the numbers unemployed one year earlier.

Mr. Jim Lester: At 9 October 1980, the latest date for which an age analysis is available, the number of young people under 20 years of age registered as unemployed in the county of South Yorkshire was 14,789. The corresponding figure at 11 October 1979 was 8,404. Hon. 330 Members will know that the youth opportunities programme exists to help these young people and that my right hon. Friend has announced a major expansion of the programme for 1981–82.

29. Mr. Madel asked the Secretary of State for Employment when he plans to meet the new chairman of the Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service to discuss codes of industrial practice; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Mayhew: Mr. Lowry's appointment does not take effect till 2 February 1981. My right hon. Friend expects to be in frequent contact with him when he assumes office. I am sure that discussions will cover, amongst other topics, the various codes of practice on industrial relations and employment matters issued both by myself and by ACAS.

31. Mr. Hal Miller asked the Secretary of State for Employment what are the numbers of employees covered by the temporary short-time working compensation scheme in the West Midlands and the country as a whole.

Mr. Jim Lester: It is not possible to provide statistics for the temporary short-time working compensation (TSTWC) scheme for the West Midlands. However, during October 1980 there were 145,500 workers working short time to save 60,519 potentially redundant jobs in the Midlands and 412,300 workers working short time to save 179,911 potentially redundant jobs throughout Great Britain as a whole.
32. Mr. Thomas Cox asked the Secretary of State for Employment what is the number of young people to the age of 18 years currently unemployed in the Greater London area.

Mr. Jim Lester: At 9 October, the latest date for which an age analysis is available, there were 20,646 young people under the age of 18 years registered as unemployed in the Greater London area. Hon. Members will know that the youth opportunities programme exists to help this group and that my right hon. Friend has announced a major expansion of the programme for 1981–82.
33. Mr. Hannam asked the Secretary of State for Employment when he expects to make a decision on the quota scheme for disabled workers.

Mr. Jim Lester: I am informed by the Manpower Services Commission that its review of the quota scheme is well advanced. I now understand that the commission will be submitting its recommendations on this complex issue to me early in the new year. I shall make no decision until I have given its advice very careful consideration.

34. Mr. Nicholas Winterton asked the Secretary of State for Employment what is his Department's estimate
331 of the numbers of workers in the United Kingdom textile and clothing industry who will have been made redundant Dr have received notices of redundancy to take effect in 1981 by the end of 1980.
Mr. Jim Lester: I regret the information is not available in the form requested.

39. Mr. Bruce-Gardyne asked the Secretary of State for Employment what representations he has received regarding his plans to change the basis of financing the industry training boards.

Mr. Jim Lester: The comments received by the MSC in its recent consultations were copied to my Department. In addition I have received comments from several organisations and individuals who wrote to me directly. The CBI, and many other employers' organisations which commented, opposed the review body's recommendation that the responsibility for funding ITB operating costs

36. Mr. Joseph Dean asked the Secretary of State for Employment what effect the changes announced in the Chancellor of the Exchequer's statement of 24 November will have on the employment prospects of school leavers in the Leeds travel to-work area.

Mr. Jim Lester: I refer the hon. Member to the earlier reply to the question from the hon. Member for Harlow (Mr. Newens). The employment prospects of school leavers are clearly related to employment prospects generally. My right hon. Friend announced on 21 November a major expansion of the youth opportunities programme to help the young unemployed in 1981–82.
38. Mr. Allan Roberts asked the Secretary of State for Employment what is the average industrial wage in the United Kingdom compared with all other European Economic Community countries.
Mr. Jim Lester: The latest available data are shown in the following table.

It is important to note that, because of differences in definitions and methods of compilation of the statistics between countries, these figures are not fully comparable. Moreover, they do not take account: of differences in taxation and social benefits, and differences in the internal purchasing power of the various national currencies.

should be transferred from the Exchequer to industry, particularly at this time. The TUC accepted the recommendation, but considered that there should be a transitional period. The Government took careful account of these and other representations in determining then-policy on the funding of ITB operating costs.
40. Mr. Heddle asked the Secretary of State for Employment what contribution wages councils are making towards reducing inflation.
Mr. Jim Lester: While a continuing falling rate of inflation is essential for economic recovery, it is doubtful whether the work of wages councils helps or hinders this trend.

Wages councils, which are independent of Government, set statutory minimum rates of pay for workers in the trades and industries they cover. These rates are determined by representatives of the trade with the help of independent members. The rates are comparatively low and in practice many employees earn more than the minimum. However, the earnings of some low paid workers are underpinned by the minima and to that extent their wages may be higher than they would be in the absence of statutory minimum rates.
41. Sir Anthony Meyer asked the Secretary of State for Employment whether he will publish statistics on a regional and sub-regional basis of the number of days lost through industrial disputes.

Mr. May hew: The regional figures as published annually in the Employment Gazette, are as follows for 1979:

44. Mr. Pavitt asked the Secretary of State for Employment how many persons are now registered as unemployed in the London borough of Brent; and what percentage increase has occurred in the last 12 months.

Mr. Jim Lester: At 13 November 1980 there were 7,809 people registered as unemployed in the area covered by the Kilburn, Wembley and Willesden employment offices, which closely corresponds to the London borough of Brent. This was 42·7 per cent. higher than the corresponding figure at 8 November 1979.

45. Mr. Homewood asked the Secretary of State for Employment how many men and how many women are registered as unemployed in the areas covered by (a) the Kettering employment office and (b) the Corby employment office.

Mr. Jim Lester: At 13 November there were 2,320 males and 856 females registered as unemployed in the Kettering employment office area. The corresponding figures for Corby were 4,792 males and 1,452 females.
Mrs. Renée Short asked the Secretary of State for Employment if he plans to introduce a 10-year programme to modernise the training and apprenticeship system; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Jim Lester: As my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Employment said in his statement to the House on 26 November we are currently discussing with the MSC and amongst those concerned in industry and education how we can make progress in modernising training arrangements, and we hope that proposals for consultation will be brought forward early in the new year. The Government are convinced that industry must take action to improve training opportunities for both adults and young people, and that greater flexibility in industrial training arrangements is essential if industry is to be able to respond effectively to the changing demands of the 1980s, and to the changing needs of individual members of the work force.
Mr. McNamara asked the Secretary of State for Employment what steps he is taking to reduce unemployment in Hull.

Mr. Jim Lester: In the longer term, employment prospects in Hull, as elsewhere in the country, depend on our success in the battle against inflation. In the meantime, Hull stands to benefit from the extra £250 million which is to be allocated nationally to the 1981–82 programme of special measures to help the unemployed. And, as a development area, Hull will continue to attract a high level of regional assistance.

Mr. Ralph Howell asked the Secretary of State for Employment, further to the reply to the hon. Member for Norfolk, North, Official Report, 6 August, column 116, if he will now estimate the net cost of employing all the unemployed, assuming a wage of £65 a week.

Mr. Jim Lester [pursuant to his reply, 1 December c. 3 1980]: Using the same assumptions that were used in the previous calculations, including benefit levels of £26·50 and April 1980 unemployment figures, the net cost would be:
All ages 18 and over

1,225 million 1,132 million

42. Mr. Wigley asked the Secretary of State for Employment what is his estimate of the additional cost to the Government for each additional man who becomes unemployed, assuming that he has a wife and two children and was previously earning the average industrial wage.
Mr. Biffen: I have been asked to reply.

The additional cost to the Government will vary according to how long the man has been unemployed. The following table, which indicates that given in the Manpower Services Commission's review and plan, 1977, therefore shows the cost for the first 12 months separately, as well as the average for the first year. The individual specified in the question, a man receiving the average
335 336 industrial wage, is not typical of the unemployed as a whole who tend to have lower than average male weekly earnings when in employment.

td.i: Financial cost to the Government of unemployment—Married man with two children

tr.td: Total Financial Cost to the Government
1. The man is assumed to be married with two children, one aged under 5, and one aged 5–10, and his wife is assumed not to be working. He becomes unemployed on 1 December 1979.

2. For each financial year, the man's earnings are assumed to be at the level of average earnings for adult males whose pay was not affected by absence, all industries and services covered by the New Earnings Survey, updated to October using the average earnings index (old series, all industries and services, adjusted). If he were not made unemployed, it is assumed his earnings would increase in April 1980 to the average level for 1980–81, assuming a 19·3 percent. increase over 1979–80. Average earnings each year are then (£per week): 1977–78:82·27; 1978–79:94·71; 1979–80: 110·81; 1980–81: 132·19.

3. Tax payments, national insurance contributions, and tax refunds are assumed to be the same in each month regardless of the number of days in the month. He is assumed not to be contracted-out of the state pension scheme.

4. Flat rate unemployment benefit is not paid for the first three days of unemployment and earnings related supplement for the first twelve. Once awarded, unemployment benefit is paid for 312 days and earnings related supplement for 156 days.

5. It is unlikely that supplementary benefit would be paid for the first few days of unemployment, pending receipt of unemployment benefits. The final wages received would be taken into consideration, and in most cases would cover requirements for this period.

6. Rent and rates: For 1979–80 rent is assumed to be £6·90 per week, and rates £2·78 per week. For 1980–81 rent is assumed to be £8·20 per week and rates £3·55 per week. (Hansard, Vol. 983, No. 167, cols. 660 et seq).

7. Income tax refunds are not counted as income when calculating entitlements to rent and rate rebates. There is no entitlement to rebates whilst in receipt of supplementary benefit, which includes an allowance for full rent and rates.

8. Net loss of indirect tax: His loss of purchasing power when unemployed compared to his position if in employment was calculated first, taking into account all transfer payments. According to the Economic Trends analysis based on the family expenditure survey—the effects of taxes and benefits on household income, 1978 Economic Trends, January 1980—for a household with around average earnings, 21·5 per cent. of disposable income in 1978 went on indirect taxes. Excluding rates, which have already been taken into account, and allowing for the offsetting effect of subsidies, gives a figure of about 18 per cent. The increase in VAT and hydrocarbon oil duty in the June 1979 Budget could be expected to raise this by about 3·5 to 21·5 per cent. in 1979–80.The April 1980 Budget is assumed to have increased the share of indirect taxes by 1per cent. of disposable income, making a total of 22·5 per cent. in 1980–81. These percentages have been applied to the loss of disposable income when unemployed to give the figures of net loss of indirect taxes in the table.

body.p: Mr. Frank Allaun asked the Secretary of State for Defence, following the crash of an RAF Nimrod aircraft in Scotland on 17 November, whether Nimrod aircraft ever carry nuclear depth charges.
Mr. Pattie: In accordance with long-standing policy, we neither confirm nor deny the presence of nuclear weapons
Mr. Tom Benyon asked the Secretary of State for Defence what was the total bill for office stationery in his Department in the last completed accounting period.

Mr. Hayhoe: The total bill for office stationery during the 1979–80 financial year was as follows:

The need for economy has recently been brought to the attention of all staff once again.

Mr. Tom Benyon asked the Secretary of State for Defence what was the total cost of servants for officer ranks in the Army, Royal Navy and Royal Air Force, respectively, in the last completed accounting period.

Mr. Mayhoe: Particular senior officers, and officers in command appointments, are entitled to a certain amount of domestic assistance, where this is required as a consequence of their official responsibilities for official entertainment and community relations. Records are not maintained separately and costs are not readily available. My noble Friend the Minister of State, Ministry of Defence will therefore write to my hon. Friend as soon as possible.
Mr. Tom Benyon asked the Secretary of State for Defence what was the total bill for drivers for the British Army of the Rhine in the last completed accounting period.

Mr. Hayhoe: The total cost of staff car drivers in BAOR during the financial year 1979–80 was approximately £3 million. The majority of these drivers are Service men often with other duties and all trained for their operational role in war.
Mr. Tom Benyon asked the Secretary of State for Defence what was the total bill for drivers for officer ranks at the Ministry of Defence in the last completed accounting period.
Mr. Hayhoe: The total cost to public funds during 1979–80 for the wages and salaries of drivers in the Ministry of Defence London car service was approximately £500,000.
Mr. Tom Benyon asked the Secretary of State for Defence what was the total bill for telephone usage for the British Army of the Rhine in the last completed accounting period.

Mr. Hayhoe: Precise figures are not available, but is is estimated that the telephone element of total communications costs for the British Army of the Rhine for the latest accounting period, covering 1 April to 31 October 1980, is some £2,150,000. The attention of all staff has recently been drawn to the expense of telecommunications and to ways of making economies.
Mr. Tom Benyon asked the Secretary of State for Defence what was the total bill for telephone usage at the Ministry of Defence in the last completed accounting period.

Mr. Hayhoe: The total bill for all Defence telephone usage at Service units, establishments and headquarters at home and overseas, for the period 1 April to 31 October 1980, was approximately £29,100,000, inclusive of VAT, of which some £4,000,000 was for MOD headquarters buildings. The figure covers rental of exchanges and other equipment, private circuits, hire of telephonists, as well as call charges. The attention of all staff has recently been drawn to this expenditure and to ways of making economies.

Mr. Tom Benyon asked the Secretary of State for Defence what was the total bill for tea ladies for all ranks and civilian employees; and what was the total number of civilian employees and Service personnel at the Ministry of Defence in the last completed accounting period and in the previous accounting period, respectively.

Mr. Hayhoe: There is no such grade as "tea lady" employed at the MOD. The average number of civilian employees and Service personnel serving at the Ministry of Defence in 1978–79 and 1979–80 was as follows:
1978–79 1979–80
Civilian employees 13,649 12,965
Service personnel 2,665 2,620

Mr. Tom Benyon asked the Secretary of State for Defence, what was; the total cost of (a) civilian employees and (b) Service personnel at the Ministry of Defence in the last completed accounting period and the previous completed accounting period, respectively.

Mr. Hayhoe: Expenditure on the pay and allowances of civilians at the Ministry of Defence was £75 million in
341 1978–79 and £88 million in 1979–80. The equivalent costs in respect of Service personnel for these years are estimated to be £22 million and £25 million respectively.

Mr. Arthur Lewis asked the Secretary of State for Defence whether he will make a statement on the sea rescue by a Sea King helicopter from the RAF Station at Brawdy in South Wales when three Irish girls were rescued from "Casper I"; what were the total costs involved; and who will meet the cost of the operation.

Mr. Pattie: At the request of Her Majesty's Coastguard at Hartland, an RAF Sea King helicopter from 202 Squadron, RAF Brawdy, was scrambled twice during the night of 25–26 November to airlift crew and passengers from the Panamanian freighter "Casper I" which had developed engine failure, and was drifting on to the coast at Port Isaac, Cornwall. The first lift, at around midnight, comprised four men and five girls, who were taken to RAF St. Mawgan. The helicopter then remained at St. Mawgan on standby while the remaining three crew members tried to weather the storm. An hour later they were also lifted back to RAF St. Mawgan. The vessel subsequently foundered.
The extra expenses incurred in the rescue total approximately £2,200. These costs will be borne by Her Majesty's Government.

Mr. Bidwell asked the Secretary of State for Defence if he will list the titles, reference numbers and dates of all circulars sent by his Department to local authorities in the last 10 years on the subject of civil defence in the event of nuclear war.
Mr. Pym: Responsibility for such circulars fall to my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for the Home Department, to whom the hon. Gentleman has already tabled an identical question.

Mr. Gordon Wilson asked the Secretary of State for Defence how nuclear waste from nuclear submarines in Scottish bases is (a) processed and (b) stored; if he will list the location of any nuclear waste dumps; and what security precautions are taken in relation to the storage of nuclear missile warheads.

Mr. Speed: Spent nuclear fuel from submarines undergoing refit in Rosyth dockyard is transported to British Nuclear Fuels Limited's plant at Windscale where it is at present stored pending a final decision on whether it is to be reprocessed. Certain other accumulated radioactive waste is moved periodically to the United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority at Harwell prior to sea dumping. Some very low-level contaminated material from the early refit programme, such as clothing, was buried at Rosyth dockyard, but all such material is now transported to BNFL's site at Drigg near Windscale for burial. All disposals are in accordance with appropriate United Kingdom and international regulations. Stringent precautions are taken to ensure the security of all nuclear weapons, but it would not be appropriate for me to go into details.

Mr. Wall asked the Secretary of State for Defence if the base for assessments of future defence expenditure will be taken as the 2½ per cent. real increase decided for the coming year or the 3 per cent. which was the original undertaking to NATO.

Mr. Pym: The undertaking to NATO is to aim for real increases in annual defence spending in the region of 3 per cent., recognising that, for some individual countries, economic circumstances would affect what could be achieved. Plans for 1982–83 and 1983–84 will be contained in the public expenditure White Paper to be published with the Budget next year.

Mr. Wm. Ross asked the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland why the licence duties set out in Statutory Rules of Northern Ireland 1980, Nos. 388 and 393, have been increased; what is the percentage increase on the former sums in each case; what has been the percentage increase in the cost of living index since the last increase; and what has been the percentage increase in the costs of running the Fisheries Conservancy Board and the Foyle Fisheries since the last increase in licence duties.
Mr. Giles Shaw: The licence duties referred to in these Statutory Rules apply only to that part of Northern Ireland under the control of the Fisheries Conservancy Board.

The board is a self-financing organisation which normally relies on licence duties as its main source of income and the increases proposed for 1981 are necessary to enable it to carry out its responsibilities under the Fisheries Act (Northern Ireland) 1966.

The percentage increase from 1980 to 1981 on the former licence duties is set out below:
(a) Eel Fishing (Licence Duties) Regulations (NI) 1980 SR 1980 No. 388: these increases vary from 29 to 30 per cent. for each type of licence.
(b) Fisheries (Licence Duties) Byelaws (Northern Ireland) 1980. SR 1980 No. 393: the increases are shown on the following table:-

body.p: Since January 1980 when the licence duties were last increased, the retail price index has increased by 13·6 per cent. The percentage increase in the cost of running the Fisheries Conservancy Board since the last increase in January 1980 is approximately 22 per cent. The cost of running the Foyle Fisheries Commission is a matter for the commission itself, but I understand that it has increased by 0·2 per cent. since the last increase in licence duties on 1 March 1980.

Mr. Wm. Ross asked the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland whether there has been an increase in the staff of the Fisheries Conservancy Board and the Foyle Fisheries Commission during the last 12 months; and, if so, how many extra staff were engaged, and for what periods by each body.
Mr. Giles Shaw: There were no increases.
Mr. Kilfedder asked the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland if he will now take action to stop the ritual slaughter of animals for export.

Mr. Giles Shaw: No. Slaughtering in accordance with Islamic and Jewish practices is permitted by law throughout the United Kingdom. However, the Farm Animal Welfare Council is considering slaughter practices in Great Britain and careful consideration will be given to any recommendation it may make.

Mr. Kilfedder asked the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland if he will ensure that the number of visitors to Northern Ireland is calculated not by the number of people who arrive in the Province by ship, aircraft or train, but by the number who stay in hotels and guest houses.

Mr. Giles Shaw: No. Many visitors do not stay in hotels and guest houses, The method used to calculate the number of visitors to Northern Ireland is the same as that employed in Great Britain and other countries and is based on internationally accepted definitions.
Mr. Kilfedder asked the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland how many visitors to' Northern Ireland stayed in hotels and guest houses, respectively, in the Province in each of the past 10 years.

Mr. Giles Shaw: I understand that the Northern Ireland Tourist Board estimates, on the basis of a sample survey, the number of visitors staying in hotels and guest houses and I will ask the chairman to write to the hon. Member.

Mr. Kilfedder asked the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland what is the total cost in the current year of the Northern Ireland Tourist Board including salaries, expenses, accommodation, travel and entertainment; and how this compares with each of the past 10 years.

Mr. Giles Shaw: The total cost to public funds, in the current financial year including salaries, expenses, accommodation, travel and entertainment is estimated at £1,632,000. The comparable total costs for the past ten years are as follows:

Details of the Northern Ireland Tourist Board's income and expenditure are contained in the board's annual accounts, copies of which for the years 1974–75 onwards are available in the Library.
Mr. Carter-Jones asked the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland what were the perinatal and infant mortality rates for Northern Ireland in 1979 and the first half of 1980 by health board areas.

Mr. Alison: I regret that this information is not yet available due to a number of factors, including industrial action by local registrars which has now ceased. When the information is available I will write to the hon. Member.

Mr. McNamara asked the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland what is the number of persons arrested
345 under the Northern Ireland (Emergency Provisions) Act and the Prevention of Terrorism (Temporary Provisions) Act in the period from September 1978 until December 1979 and from January 1980 to the nearest convenient date; for how long those arrested were interrogated; and what proportion were subsequently charged with an offence, scheduled or unscheduled and which offence.

Mr. Humphrey Atkins [pursuant to his reply, 3 December 1980]: The number of arrests under the Prevention of Terrorism (Temporary Provisions) Act 1976, and persons subsequently charged, during the periods in question are as follows:—
Period Arrests Persons Charged
1.9.78 to 31.12.79 214 72
1.1.80 to 31.10.80 201 95

Because of the method of maintaining records prior to 1980, it is not possible except at disproportionate cost to identify the number of arrests under the Northern Ireland (Emergency Provisions) Act 1978, or the number of persons subsequently charged, for the period 1 September 1978 to 31 December 1979. During the period 1 January 1980 to 31 October 1980, a total of 3,868 arrests were made under the Act. Of these 577 were re-arrests by the police of people initially arrested by the Army. Three hundred and thirty three persons were charged with scheduled offences and 41 with unscheduled offences as a result.
It is not possible except at disproportionate cost to identify the length of time for which persons arrested were held or the specific offences with which those concerned were charged.

Mr. Freeson asked the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland if he will make a statement on the physical and mental condition of Pauline McLaughlin currently in Armagh prison hospital; and if he will release her to a civilian hospital.

Mr. Humphrey Atkins [pursuant to his reply, 4 December 1980]: Pauline McLaughlin was first remanded to prison in 1976 and sentenced early in 1978 to detention during the pleasure of the Secretary of State for the murder of a soldier in 1974. She was also sentenced to concurrent terms of imprisonment ranging from 5 to 16 years for seven other offences, including attempted murder and causing explosions.

It is on record that before her imprisonment she already suffered from a condition of nervous origin which manifested itself in the form of repeated vomiting. Since her admission to Armagh prison this vomiting has caused gradual loss of weight. She has had thorough medical investigation and treatment both within the prison and in hospital outside. Her psychological state and the effects of her vomiting on her weight and bodily functions continue to cause concern and she is being carefully observed by professional staff. Her condition is not at present critical. She is not in the prison hospital.

Throughout her imprisonment this girl has had the most assiduous and expert medical attention from prison medical staff backed up by the facilities and specialist expertise of the Health Service. She has had frequent 346 examinations by outside consultants, including one nominated by solicitors acting for her family, who have expressed their approval and high regard for the health care she has received in prison.

While Miss McLaughlin's health does give cause for serious concern, it is considered in the light of all the advice available that there are insufficient grounds for taking the exceptional course of releasing her on licence from the indeterminate sentence and using the Royal Prerogative to remit the balance of the fixed terms. However, the case will continue to be kept under very close review, and if at any time Miss McLaughlin requires treatment which cannot be provided in the prison she will be moved to the most suitable outside hospital without delay.

Statements have recently been circulated to the effect that necessary health care has been denied to this prisoner. These are wholly untrue. The professional staff in attendance act solely in accordance with clinical judgment and professional ethics and the prison administration puts no obstacles in the way of medical assessment and treatment.

Mr. Michael Brown asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer what would be the extra costs, on the assumption that invalidity pensions were already treated on taxable income, of extending the age allowance to invalidity pensioners.
Mr. Peter Rees: If invalidity pensions had been taxable in 1980–81 it is estimated that the cost of extending the age allowance to invalidity pensioners would have been of the order of £35 million.

Mr. Bright asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer how many Inland Revenue officers have been subject to disciplinary proceedings for actions displaying incompetence or lack of courtesy to the public in the year ended 31 March 1980.
Mr. Peter Rees: 18 officers were disciplined for incompetence, and one for lack of courtesy.

Mr. Austin Mitchell asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether he will publish in the Official Report the estimated increase in the money supply in the first half of 1980, taking account of disintermediation; and if he will indicate when he expects this to be reflected in a corresponding increase in the rate of inflation.

Mr. Lawson: The seasonally adjusted increase in sterling M3 for the first six banking months of 1980 was 11·2 per cent. at an annual rate. After adjusting for distortions caused by the operation of the corset and its removal in June the underlying growth rate was probably somewhat higher. It is, however, not possible to measure it precisely, particularly from month to month. Estimates of distortions are inherently unreliable and would be liable to frequent change as more information became available. On the basis of our best assessment to date, it seems likely that the growth of sterling M3 during the current target period has been of the order of 20 per cent. per annum in underlying terms.
Future rates of inflation will depend on monetary developments over an extended period and short-run fuctuations in monetary growth probably have relatively little impact.
Mr. Richard Page asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer what is the yield of value added tax on funeral companies.

Mr. Peter Rees: The information is not available. Burials and cremations are exempt from VAT and businesses are not required to register for VAT unless they also make supplies of taxable goods and services exceeding in value the exemption limit, now £13,500 a year. In 1979–80 VAT amounting to £1·4 million was charged to their customers by businesses registered as funeral directors, cemeteries and crematoria.

Mr. Wheeler asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer if he will list in the Official Report details of the market research into the currency and coinage requirements of commerce and the general public carried out by his Department or the Royal Mint over the past five years.
Mr. Lawson: No. The market research has been carried out by the Royal Mint and not the Treasury and much of it provides a basis for commercial decisions or confidential advice to Ministers.
Mr. McCrindle asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether he proposes any change in the income tax arrangements which apply to the occupation of woodlands managed on a commercial basis.

Sir Geoffrey Howe: I have been considering this matter in the light of the comments and recommendation of the Public Accounts Committe in its eighth report. The present taxation arrangements for woodlands have existed for a considerable time and I recognise the important part which they play in encouraging investment by the private sector in the industry. It is particularly important in an industry with the long timescale of forestry for there to be stability in the tax arrangements so that confidence is maintained. In the light of these considerations, I have concluded that no change should be made to the present income tax arrangements.
Mr. Dykes asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer what was the real cost to the Exchequer of providing tax relief
on payments made into private pension schemes in each of the years 1975–76, 1976–77, 1977–78, 1978–79 and 1979–80 respectively.

Mr. Peter Rees [pursuant to his reply, 8 December 1980]: The net cost of all income tax reliefs for occupational pension schemes is estimated to be:

These figures are subject to a wide margin of eror. They live been calculated on the basis set out in the Inland Revenue's note of February 1978 to the General Sub-Committee of the Expenditure Committee—second report 1977–78, appendix 15.

Mr. McQuarrie asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer what is the daily financial contribution by the British Government to the funds of the European Economic Community; and if he will list the annual increase in these payments for the years 1977, 1978 and 1979.

Mr. Lawson [pursuant to his reply, 8 December 1980]: The United Kingdom's net contributions in the years quoted were £368·4 million, £803·9 million and £943·3 million respectively. On a daily basis the figures were as follows:
Average Daily net Contribution
Increase over previous years
